newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr shows baht positive side of floating.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr shows baht positive side of floating.

text.p: As the Thai baht contemplates life under a floating regime, the experience of the Australian dollar shows that while wild swings are inevitable volatility does recede with time.

And analysts argue that in the 14 years since the dollar was set free, it has added a discipline to economic decision-making which has discouraged profligate policies and forced Australia to address its national savings imbalance.
"You would be hard-pressed to find an economist to say the experience of floating has not been a good one for Australia," said John Kyriakopoulos, a senior economist at J.P. Morgan.
The dollar's early experience after financial deregulation in December 1983 was not a happy one as it crumbled from over 94 U.S. cents to under 65 cents in little more than a year.
But neither had the managed regime prevented poor fundamentals from making themselves felt -- at the start of 1982, for instance, the dollar had been worth US$1.1000.

The nadir was reached in 1986 when a ballooning budget deficit, labour market strife, rampant inflation and, above all, an explosion in Australia's current account deficit led to a now infamous outburst from the then Treasurer Paul Keating.
In an off-the-cuff remark he warned Australia was at risk of becoming a "banana republic" if its trade deficit was not dealt with.
Offshore investors, alarmed by such candour, dumped the dollar in a wild selling spree which saw it reach an all-time low around 59 cents in July that year.
But economists reckoned the crisis proved cathartic in the end in that it forced the government to take the tough economic decisions which were needed.
"A floating rate is a constraint on pursuing policies which are not sound," said Kyrikopoulos. "In some ways the market was acting as a policeman -- and it worked."
